# Technical Building Blocks



An AI-native design system stands on four technical building blocks (@tbl-part-ii-roadmap): machine-usable representations of design state, method selection across learned and conventional approaches, tool-connected execution environments, and verification feedback that qualifies what the tools return. A language model connected to a hardware generator without them produces syntactically plausible designs that no physical check has touched.

The tension running through all four is machine usability against physical ground truth. A fast surrogate accelerates search by orders of magnitude and, left unchecked, rewards the candidates its own errors flatter; @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization names that failure, and @sec-feedback-verification-trust supplies the qualification rules that keep it out of the project record. The chapters in between show which representations preserve the constraints a method must respect and how a learned method reaches a cycle-accurate simulator or a signoff tool without corrupting the state it depends on.


::: {.callout-part}
1. Which structural representations preserve hardware constraints and domain rules during automated search? (@sec-data-representations-world-models)
2. When should an architect select conventional analysis over learned surrogates, generative models, or black-box optimizers? (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization)
3. How do typed execution harnesses isolate deterministic simulator state from the search that drives them? (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces)
4. What qualification rules keep a proxy result from being recorded as an architecture outcome? (@sec-feedback-verification-trust)
:::

## Governing Design Principles {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Seven design principles govern the technical foundation of Part II. Each draws a boundary across representation, method selection, execution isolation, or verification, so that an automated exploration loop produces results a reviewer can inspect rather than optimization artifacts no tool has checked:

- **@sec-data-representations-world-models:** Represent What Decisions Must Preserve, and Bind Observations to Generating Context. A method can act only on the properties its input representation exposes, and an observation loses authority the moment it is separated from its register-transfer level (RTL) revision, compiler flags, workload trace, tool version, and operating conditions.
- **@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization:** Select the Smallest Sufficient Method. A learned model is never adopted where conventional analysis, a deterministic solver, or direct simulation already satisfies the decision's evidence requirement.
- **@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces:** Automate Within Recoverable Boundaries, and Unrecorded Runs Cannot Justify Claims. Wrappers and harnesses enforce isolated tool boundaries, explicit budgets, and complete lineage, and a returned value with no execution record cannot enter a comparison.
- **@sec-feedback-verification-trust:** Stronger Claims Require Stronger Checks, and Drive Actions Only from Qualified Results. Verification effort scales with the consequence and reversibility of the claim, and only a qualified status justifies a repair, a revision, a no-change decision, or a stop.

## Chapter Roadmap {.unnumbered .unlisted}

The four chapters of Part II assemble the foundation in order, from representations of design state through method selection and tool containment to verification feedback. @tbl-part-ii-roadmap organizes the architecture question and the deliverable of each chapter:

| **Chapter** | **Core Architecture Question** | **Key Takeaway / Deliverable** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **@sec-data-representations-world-models** | What does an AI-native design system need to know, where does that information come from, and how should it be represented? | Classifies the representations that make design state machine-usable (syntax trees, dataflow graphs, transaction-level models), the context each observation must carry, and the difference between durable project knowledge and live design state. |
| **@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization** | What job should AI perform, which method suits it, and when is a conventional method or no AI better? | Separates the engineering role from the method family and technique, and applies the smallest sufficient method rule with conventional analysis as a serious outcome. |
| **@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces** | What is an architecture design environment, and what must it provide for AI-native work? | Builds the tool, wrapper, harness, and environment split with pinned state, typed contracts, and execution records. |
| **@sec-feedback-verification-trust** | How do returned signals become trustworthy, what do they mean for the work, and what should improve or be retained? | Qualifies returned signals before they support a claim, routes each qualified result to the action it justifies, and separates what a run should improve from what the project retains. |
: **Part II chapter roadmap across representations, methods, environments, and feedback.** The four building blocks are what a closed-loop exploration needs before it can run against real design tools. {#tbl-part-ii-roadmap tbl-colwidths="[20,40,40]"}

Together, these four chapters turn the ambition of Part I into components an engineer can build and check. The foundation begins in @sec-data-representations-world-models with the representations that make hardware design state usable by a method at all.
